newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's opposition piles pressure on Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's opposition piles pressure on Milosevic.

text.p: Serbia's opposition piled on the pressure on President Slobodan Milosevic to reverse alleged election fraud as the West attempted to defuse a crisis some fear could result in bloodshed.
More than 200,000 opposition supporters rallied in Belgrade on Saturday in the biggest demonstration in more than three weeks of peaceful anti-government street protests.

Belgrade students earlier staged their biggest demonstration in weeks, with reporters estimating that up to 40,000 protesters marched through the streets to the cheers of people lining the pavement or waving from windows and balconies.

Serbia's opposition and students have held daily street protests since the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition claimed it was cheated of victory in local elections in November in major towns and cities, including Belgrade.
Milosevic has remained largely silent apart from inviting a team of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to look into the matter.

European Union leaders meeting in Dublin set conditions for the OSCE team, backed by Washington, to verify the regularity of last month's polls, including the right to re-run them under international supervision, mediator Carl Bildt said.

Some diplomats fear too much pressure on Milosevic could cause a bloodbath in Serbia, an image the authorities are quietly keen to foster as a deterrent to the opposition. But police have so far kept a low profile in face of the protests.

In addition to the Belgrade demonstrations, thousands of people held protests in 17 major towns and cities which with their industrial and cultural resources make up the so-called backbone of Serbia, independent reports said.

The authorities, minimising the size of the protests, argued that the number of demonstrators accounted for less than 10 percent of Belgrade's population of two million or Serbia's population of 10 million.

But Milosevic's chances of sitting out the crisis until the demontrations died down appeared to be fading in view of the tenacity of the opposition and its attraction to many people still reluctant to physically join the protests.
"Not only they are not diminishing but they are gradually growing in size and spreading across Serbia. Milosevic will have to make his move very soon," a Western diplomat said.
One of Zajedno's leaders, Zoran Djindjic, said: "We are at the beginning of a long road to the future -- we can discuss the pace at which we will move, but definitely not the direction."
Vuk Draskovic, a fellow Zajedno leader, said: "We had all lost all hope as individuals, but together we restored that hope. All of Serbia will soon be out in the streets."
Bildt pinned blame for the crisis on Milosevic and sent a message of support to the Belgrade students.
"By your actions you are showing Europe and the world that Serbia one day -- hopefully not far away -- is willing and able to join the family of open and free Eruropean democracies," he said.
